title: Are Jailbreak Attacks More Effective on Longer or Shorter System Prompts?

original_idea.problem: Whether longer system prompts provide more or less jailbreak resistance is uninvestigated.
original_idea.direction: Test 3 attack types with: no system prompt, 1-sentence, 10-sentence, and 50-sentence safety policy. Measure ASR per condition across 30 prompts.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If longer system prompts reduce safety by creating more reasoning context, deployers may be making themselves more vulnerable.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: system prompt length -> safety effectiveness -> deployment guidance. Practical but the causal mechanism is underspecified and the fix would be indirect.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Very simple: vary system prompt length, run attacks, measure ASR. Standard API usage. No ML training. Beginner-accessible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: 4 system prompt conditions x 3 attack types, measure ASR. Single experiment with obvious deliverable. Quick to execute.

novelty.reasoning: While system prompts are recognized as a defensive mechanism, the specific relationship between system prompt length and jailbreak ASR has not been systematically studied. The 'Bag of Tricks' paper (NeurIPS 2024) identifies system prompt as a model-level factor but does not provide a controlled length ablation. Existing research notes that safe system prompts enhance robustness but does not characterize whether this scales with length or whether longer prompts create more reasoning context that attackers can exploit. The proposed 4-condition experiment (none, 1-sentence, 10-sentence, 50-sentence) with 3 attack types is a clean, novel ablation.

evidence: Bag of Tricks: Benchmarking of Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs. NeurIPS 2024.
SequentialBreak: LLMs Can be Fooled by Embedding Jailbreak Prompts into Sequential Prompt Chains. arXiv:2411.06426, 2024.
